opus-5.5.text:
Being at Google, even part-time, gave me a very concrete sense of what scale really means. You see teams with thousands of accelerators and huge, well-organized data pipelines, and the engineering is excellent. There's a whole machine around training very large models, and it works.

The first lesson was humbling. If a direction mainly comes down to "who can train the biggest model on the most data," academia shouldn't compete head-on there. We'll lose, and arguably we shouldn't even try. Spending a whole PhD replicating a slightly smaller version of what an industry lab will release in three months isn't a good use of a student's life.

The second lesson was more encouraging. Being inside showed me where the blind spots are. When an organization commits to a roadmap at that scale, it naturally becomes conservative about the fundamentals. The architecture, the objective, the representation are often taken as given, because changing them is expensive and risky. That's exactly where academia has an advantage. We can ask the "what if this basic assumption is wrong?" questions. What if we don't need this component? What if visual representation should be learned differently? What if the recipe everyone copies isn't actually optimal?

So I tried to steer my group toward problems that are fundamental and still under-explored. Representation learning, how vision and language should really fit together, what the right architecture for generative models is, how models should understand space and the physical world rather than just text. Those questions don't require being the biggest player. They require good taste, careful experiments, and the freedom to be wrong for a while.

There's also a mindset part. Industry rewards shipping, and academia should reward insight. I tell my students not to chase leaderboards. Try to find something that, once you show it, makes people say, "oh, we should all be doing it this way." Seeing how industry works up close made me more confident about that division of labor. The two sides are complementary, and academia is most useful when it acts like academia, not like a small, underfunded version of an industry lab.

r001.rationale: He says seeing Google’s large-scale training work showed him academia should avoid competing to train the biggest models or spending a PhD replicating industry work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a bit of a shock at first. When I was at FAIR and then visiting places like Google, you see the scale they operate at. Thousands of TPUs, data pipelines that an academic lab could never dream of building. And my first reaction was almost discouraging, like, how do I compete with this?

But after a while, I realized that was the wrong framing. The question isn't how to compete, it's what they structurally cannot do, or won't do, because of how incentives work in industry. Big labs are very good at scaling things that already work. If you give them a recipe, they'll push it ten times, a hundred times further. What they're less good at is sitting with a question that has no obvious product payoff for two or three years, or questioning an assumption the whole field already agreed on.

So that shaped my choices quite a lot. I decided to focus on things where understanding matters more than scale. Representation learning, what the model actually learns inside, why one architecture generalizes differently from another. Things like ConvNeXt came from a question like that. Everyone was saying transformers won, convolution is dead. And we just asked, is that really the architecture, or is it the training recipe? You don't need a giant cluster to ask that question. You need a careful experiment design.

The other thing I took from Google was humility about data and evaluation. Internally, people know very well where the benchmarks are broken, but they often don't have time to fix them because the roadmap moves on. In academia, that's exactly the kind of work we can do: build the evaluation, define the problem properly, and then let the industry labs scale it.

So I'd say the influence was less about copying their directions and more about choosing the complementary ones. I want my students to work on problems where the bottleneck is an idea, not a GPU budget.

r001.rationale: The response says his experiences at Google shaped his choices and led him toward complementary research, but it does not clearly state that he sought to learn what Google was working on in order to identify directions to avoid in academia.

astra-6.text:
Seeing what people at Google were doing made me think more carefully about where I could contribute in academia. If a direction depended mainly on having more compute, more data, or a huge engineering team, it would be difficult for a university lab to compete on those terms. So I wanted to look for questions where a small team could make progress through a good idea or a carefully designed experiment.

That doesn’t necessarily mean working on something small. You can ask a very fundamental question about how a model works or whether a particular design choice is actually necessary. Academia gives you room to step back and question assumptions. For me, that became an important way to choose research directions: where can we offer a different perspective, and what can we learn with the resources we have?

r001.rationale: The response says Google’s work prompted him to seek research areas where academia could contribute, especially with limited resources. It does not state that he sought to identify Google’s research directions in order to avoid pursuing them.

sol-6.1.text:
Seeing what people at Google were doing helped me think about where academic research could have the most impact. In industry, you have resources, infrastructure, and practical problems at a scale that’s difficult to reproduce in a university. So I didn’t want to choose a direction where the main question was simply whether we could use more computation or more data.

Instead, I became more interested in the ideas underneath: What makes a representation useful? Which design choices actually matter? Can we find a simpler way to achieve the same thing? Those are questions where a small academic group can still make a meaningful contribution. It wasn’t about avoiding problems that industry cared about—it was about finding an angle where a good experiment or a different perspective could change how people approached the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Google’s work helped identify where academic research could have impact and that he avoided directions centered mainly on more compute or data. It does not say he sought to identify and avoid research directions based on what Google was working on.
